title: Strength Training for Middle- and Long-Distance Performance: A Meta-Analysis
authors: Berryman N, Mujika I, Arvisais D, Roubeix M, Binet C, Bosquet L
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
population: Endurance athletes in running, cycling, cross-country skiing and swimming; 28 of 554 potential studies included
findings: 28 of 554 potential studies met inclusion criteria; subgroups examined strength-training intensity, duration, frequency, performance level, age, sex and sport.
A strength-training mesocycle was associated with a moderate improvement in middle- and long-distance performance (net SMD 0.52, 95% CI 0.33-0.70).
Associated improvements were seen in energy cost of locomotion (SMD 0.65, 0.32-0.98), maximal force (0.99, 0.80-1.18) and maximal power (0.50, 0.34-0.67).
Maximal-force training led to greater improvements than other intensities; beneficial effects on performance were consistent irrespective of the athletes' level.
limitations: Pools running with cycling, skiing and swimming, so running-specific effect is not isolated in the abstract; sample size not stated in abstract; mixed study quality not summarized in the abstract.
implications: Supports maximal-force (heavy) training as the preferred intensity for performance across endurance sports.
Supports offering strength work at all performance levels, not only elite runners.

verification.notes: Added by verifier. Crossref (IJSPP, 2018, Berryman) and Europe PMC abstract checked. Pooled across sports, so graded for running indirectly.
